titleStmt.title: How the machine ‘thinks’: Understanding opacity in machine learning algorithms
titleStmt.author: Jenna Burrell

bibl.title: How the machine ‘thinks’: Understanding opacity in machine learning algorithms

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: opacity in socially consequential algorithmic classification - spam filters, credit scoring, fraud detection, search ranking - and specifically what makes machine learning classifiers hard to understand
span.quote: This article considers the issue of opacity as a problem for socially consequential mechanisms of classification and ranking, such as spam filters, credit card fraud detection, search engines, news trends, market segmentation and advertising, insurance or loan qualification, and credit scoring. These mechanisms of classification all frequently rely on computational algorithms, and in many cases on _machine learning_ algorithms to do this work. In this article, I draw a distinction between three forms of opacity: (1) opacity as intentional corporate or state secrecy, (2) opacity as technical illiteracy, and (3) an opacity that arises from the characteristics of machine learning algorithms and the scale required to apply them usefully. The analysis in this article gets inside the algorithms themselves. I cite existing literatures in computer science, known industry practices (as they are publicly presented), and do some testing and manipulation of code as a form of lightweight code audit. I argue that recognizing the distinct forms of opacity that may be coming into play in a given application is a key to determining which of a variety of technical and non-technical solutions could help to prevent harm. This article considers the issue of opacity as a problem for socially consequential mechanisms of classification and ranking, such as spam filters, credit card fraud detection, search engines, news trends, market segmentation and advertising, insurance or loan qualification, and credit scoring. These are just some examples of mechanisms of classification

span.label: what the reasons are for not knowing how a classification was arrived at - proprietary secrecy, technical difficulty, or something else
span.quote: They are opaque in the sense that if one is a recipient of the output of the algorithm (the classification decision), rarely does one have any concrete sense of how or why a particular classification has been arrived at from inputs.

span.label: a three-way typology of opacity - corporate secrecy, technical illiteracy, and the mismatch between high-dimensional optimisation and human interpretation - with the argument that each form needs a different remedy
span.quote: In this article, I draw a distinction between three forms of opacity: (1) opacity as intentional corporate or state secrecy, (2) opacity as technical illiteracy, and (3) an opacity that arises from the characteristics of machine learning algorithms and the scale required to apply them usefully.

span.label: method
span.quote: I argue that recognizing the distinct forms of opacity that may be coming into play in a given application is a key to determining which of a variety of technical and non-technical solutions could help to prevent harm.

span.label: the recipient of an algorithmic classification rarely has any concrete sense of how or why it was arrived at
span.quote: They are opaque in the sense that if one is a recipient of the output of the algorithm (the classification decision), rarely does one have any concrete sense of how or why a particular classification has been arrived at from inputs.

span.label: citation of computer science literature and known industry practice, plus testing and manipulation of code as a lightweight code audit, worked through handwriting recognition and spam filtering examples
span.term: citation of computer science literature and known industry practice, plus testing and manipulation of code as a lightweight code audit, worked through handwriting recognition and spam filtering examples
span.quote: I cite existing literatures in computer science, known industry practices (as they are publicly presented), and do some testing and manipulation of code as a form of lightweight code audit.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE MACHINE BUILDS ITS OWN REPRESENTATION WITHOUT REGARD FOR HUMAN COMPREHENSION - optimisation over training data does not naturally accord with human semantic explanation, so the opacity is a property of the method and not of anyone's choice or skill
span.quote: When a computer learns and consequently builds its own representation of a classification decision, it does so without regard for human comprehension. Machine optimizations based on training data do not naturally accord with human semantic explanations.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: USEFULNESS REQUIRES COMPLEXITY: a machine learning algorithm CAN be implemented so its logic is fully comprehensible, but such an instance is unlikely to be useful - accuracy carries a degree of unavoidable complexity
span.quote: Though a machine learning algorithm can be implemented simply in such a way that its logic is almost fully comprehensible, in practice, such an instance is unlikely to be particularly useful. Machine learning models that prove useful (specifically, in terms of the ‘accuracy’ of classification) possess a degree of unavoidable complexity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE OPACITY IS IN THE INTERPLAY, NOT IN EITHER PART: the dataset may be large but comprehensible and the code may be written with clarity, and the complexity arises between them, in the mechanism of the algorithm operating on data
span.quote: While datasets may be extremely large but possible to comprehend and code may be written with clarity, the interplay between the two in the mechanism of the algorithm is what yields the complexity (and thus opacity).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE DECISION LOGIC CHANGES AS THE ALGORITHM LEARNS, so reading the code as written does not tell you what it does after training
span.quote: The internal decision logic of the algorithm is altered as it ‘learns’ on training data.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: DIMENSIONALITY MANIPULATION BREAKS THE FEATURE-TO-DIMENSION CORRESPONDENCE: with PCA or the kernel trick the relation is not one-to-one, so a 'weighted input' can no longer be traced to a human-readable property
span.quote: it is often the case that the relationship between a feature and a dimension in the model is not one-to-one.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: INTUITION FAILS AT HIGH DIMENSIONS - each of thousands of features subtly and imperceptibly shifts the classification, so debugging and improvement get harder as inputs are added
span.note: status: Domingos (2012) notes that ‘intuition fails at high-dimensions.’
span.quote: Domingos (2012) notes that ‘intuition fails at high-dimensions.’ In other words, reasoning about, debugging, or improving the algorithm becomes more difficult with more qualities or characteristics provided as inputs, each subtly and imperceptibly shifting the resulting classification.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SOME ALGORITHMS ARE OPAQUE IN ORDER TO WORK: spam, scam and fraud detection face an adversary who adapts, so disclosure would defeat the system - opacity here is functional rather than merely protective
span.quote: Network security applications of machine learning deal explicitly with spam, scams, and fraud and remain opaque in order to be effective.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SECRECY MAY BE COVER RATHER THAN COMPETITIVE NECESSITY: Pasquale's reading is that the adversary is regulation itself, which makes the same observable opacity a different problem with a different remedy
span.note: status: he argues that a kind of adversarial situation is indeed in play
span.quote: he argues that a kind of adversarial situation is indeed in play, one where the adversary is regulation itself.

span.label: the audit's explanation was produced by imposing human interpretive reasoning on a process of statistical optimisation - 'machine thinking was resolved to human interpretation' - which the author flags as a limit of his own method
span.quote: probing further into the ‘why’ of a particular classification decision yielded suggestive evidence that seemed sufficient as an explanation, but this imposed a process of human interpretive reasoning on a mathematical process of statistical optimization. In other words, machine thinking was resolved to human interpretation.

span.label: ambiguities remained after the audit and the author doubts the explanation was necessarily a correct one
span.quote: Yet ambiguities remained, such as the weighting of innocuous words like ‘visit’ and ‘want’ as indicators for spam. This raises doubts about whether an explanation produced in this way to satisfy the ‘why’ question was necessarily a particularly correct one.

span.label: end-user explanations that list a few key criteria are at best incomplete and at worst false reassurance - which applies to the remedy the paper is closest to endorsing
span.quote: explanations that bring forward a human-manageable list of key criteria (i.e. the 10 most heavily weighted/spammy words present in an email or a single sentence description) provide an understanding that is at best incomplete16 and at worst false reassurance.

span.label: the paper's own examples are handwriting recognition and spam filtering, where the feature-to-dimension relation IS one-to-one, and it states that this is often not the case
span.quote: it is often the case that the relationship between a feature and a dimension in the model is not one-to-one.

span.label: no single tool or process will alleviate black-boxed classification, and the right combination is said to depend on the application space rather than being specified
span.quote: Alleviating problems of black boxed classification will not be accomplished by a single tool or process, but some combination of regulations or audits (of the code itself and, more importantly, of the algorithms functioning), the use of alternatives that are more transparent (i.e. open source), education of the general public as well as the sensitization of those bestowed with the power to write such consequential code.

span.label: the difficulty is stated to persist even for those with specialised training and even for computer scientists, which bounds what any literacy remedy can achieve
span.quote: The examples of handwriting recognition and spam filtering helped to illustrate how the workings of machine learning algorithms can escape full understanding and interpretation by humans, even for those with specialized training, even for computer scientists.

span.label: the code audit found the word 'Nigeria' neutrally weighted in the spam classifier - a check that produced reassuring evidence rather than the expected discriminatory finding, and the paper reports it that way
span.note: eliminates: discriminatory weighting of the word `Nigeria` as the explanation of the spam classifier's behaviour - the audit found it neutrally weighted · outcome: partial
span.quote: probing further into the ‘why’ of a particular classification decision yielded suggestive evidence that seemed sufficient as an explanation, but this imposed a process of human interpretive reasoning on a mathematical process of statistical optimization. In other words, machine thinking was resolved to human interpretation.

span.label: the author states plainly that the explanation his own audit produced may not be correct: innocuous words like 'visit' and 'want' were weighted as spam indicators and remained unexplained
span.note: eliminates: the audit's own explanation being taken as a description of what the classifier does, when words the author calls innocuous carry spam weight and remain unaccounted for · outcome: failed
span.quote: Yet ambiguities remained, such as the weighting of innocuous words like ‘visit’ and ‘want’ as indicators for spam. This raises doubts about whether an explanation produced in this way to satisfy the ‘why’ question was necessarily a particularly correct one.

span.label: semantic interpretation
span.quote: Three distinct forms of opacity include: (1) opacity as intentional corporate or institutional self-protection and concealment and, along with it, the possibility for knowing deception; (2) opacity stemming from the current state of affairs where writing (and reading) code is a specialist skill and; (3) an opacity that stems from the mismatch between mathematical optimization in high-dimensionality characteristic of machine learning and the demands of human-scale reasoning and styles of semantic interpretation.

span.label: spam
span.quote: Network security applications of machine learning deal explicitly with spam, scams, and fraud and remain opaque in order to be effective.

span.label: opacity - THREE DIFFERENT THINGS UNDER ONE WORD, and the paper's whole point is that they are routinely conflated: (1) intentional corporate or state secrecy, (2) the fact that reading code is a specialist skill, (3) the mismatch between high-dimensional mathematical optimisation and human-scale semantic reasoning. Only the third is intrinsic to machine learning
span.quote: Three distinct forms of opacity include: (1) opacity as intentional corporate or institutional self-protection and concealment and, along with it, the possibility for knowing deception; (2) opacity stemming from the current state of affairs where writing (and reading) code is a specialist skill and; (3) an opacity that stems from the mismatch between mathematical optimization in high-dimensionality characteristic of machine learning and the demands of human-scale reasoning and styles of semantic interpretation.

span.label: opacity - AND THE SECOND AND THIRD SENSES ARE THE PAIR THAT GET CONFUSED, both reading as 'this is technical and complex'. The paper separates them because they have opposite remedies: education fixes illiteracy and cannot touch dimensionality
span.quote: This third form of opacity (often conflated with the second form as part of the general sense that algorithms and code are very technical and complex) is the particular focus of this article.

span.label: opacity (Pasquale's sense) - 'REMEDIABLE INCOMPREHENSIBILITY', which builds the remedy into the definition. Burrell's third form is precisely the case that definition cannot cover, since no disclosure makes it comprehensible
span.quote: In reference to this, he defines ‘opacity’ as ‘remediable incomprehensibility.’

span.label: code audit - IN THIS PAPER, TWO INCOMPATIBLE THINGS: reading the source, which is what the legal literature proposes, and observing the algorithm in action on data, which is what the third form of opacity actually requires. The paper's critique of audits turns entirely on which one is meant
span.quote: These are challenges not just of reading and comprehending code, but being able to understand the algorithm in action, operating on data.
